Q004655:
## What an AIP Logic function is
AIP Logic is Palantir's no-code way to build an LLM-powered function. It has typed inputs and outputs, a system prompt and a task prompt with injected variables, and blocks that can call tools, branch or loop. A function can also make Ontology edits, so its output changes real objects.
## Why versions and traces matter
Applications and automations call a **published version**. Each run leaves an execution trace: the exact prompt after variables were injected, every tool call and its result, the raw model output and the edit that was applied. When behaviour changes right after an edit, the trace shows which stage changed instead of leaving you to guess.
- Classify the failure first: prompt design, block wiring, tool configuration, model behaviour or execution logic.
- Protect consumers: they should stay on the last known-good version while you debug.
- Example: if the new prompt says "flag anything mentioning pressure as urgent", the trace will show that sentence driving the urgent output on routine pressure checks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger model:** a stronger model still follows the edited prompt, so a prompt that now asks for the wrong thing keeps producing the wrong priority. It adds cost without finding the cause.
- ✗ **B. Rewrite in code:** AIP Logic runs can be debugged through their traces and earlier versions stay available. Rewriting in code throws away working logic and still does not explain what the prompt edit broke.
- ✗ **C. Higher temperature:** temperature adds randomness to the output; it does not fix a changed instruction and makes priorities less consistent. Publishing at once also pushes an untested change to every consumer.
- ✓ **D. Trace comparison with a known-good version (correct):** the problem appeared right after a prompt change, so the trace of a failing ticket against the previous version locates the stage that broke. Keeping consumers on that version stops wrong priorities reaching the Ontology while the fix is tested.

## Key idea
When an AI function changes behaviour, read the trace against the last good version and keep consumers on that version until the fix is proven.
Q004656:
## What the agent has to get right
An AIP agent combines a model, instructions, retrieval context and tools. This one can do two kinds of things: answer from manuals (read) and create a work order (write). The write tool is where a mistake has real consequences.
## A release test set
The exam guide asks for testing with representative, edge and adversarial interactions before release. A practical set for this agent:
- Typical: common fault questions the manuals cover.
- Edge: a model not in the manuals, two manuals that disagree, a question with missing information.
- Insufficient evidence: the agent should say it cannot find support, not invent a procedure.
- Write path: a request missing required fields, a user without permission to create work orders, an instruction hidden inside a pasted log.
Run these before launch and keep them as a regression suite for every later change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Prompt instruction:** a sentence in the prompt cannot guarantee behaviour and gives no evidence of quality. Controls on the tool and a tested refusal path do; the prompt is not a test.
- ✗ **B. Use production as the test:** users would meet unsafe answers and wrong work orders first. Production feedback is valuable for improving the suite, but it does not replace testing before release.
- ✓ **C. Typical, edge and adversarial cases (correct):** a demo only shows the happy path. Production failures come from unanswerable questions, conflicting sources and misuse of the write tool, so those cases must be tested before technicians rely on the agent.
- ✗ **D. Rephrased demo questions:** this measures consistency on easy questions only. It never checks what the agent does when evidence is missing or when the work order tool is misused.

## Key idea
Before releasing an agent, test typical, edge, insufficient-evidence and adversarial cases, with extra focus on tools that change data.
Q004657:
## How semantic search works
An embedding model turns text into a vector, a list of numbers that places similar meanings close together. At indexing time every chunk is embedded and stored, for example as a vector property on an object. At query time the question is embedded and the nearest chunk vectors are returned.
## Why the model must match
Each embedding model builds its own vector space. Distances are only meaningful between vectors from the same model, so a query vector from model B compared with chunk vectors from model A gives nearly random neighbours.
- The exam guide states the rule directly: use the same embedding model for indexing and query-time retrieval.
- Example: "parental leave eligibility" embedded with the new model may land closest to an expense policy chunk embedded with the old one.
When you upgrade the model, re-embed the corpus, rebuild the index, then switch queries, and compare retrieval quality on an evaluation set before and after.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mismatched embedding models (correct):** query and chunk vectors from different models are not comparable, which explains a sudden drop right after the switch. Re-embedding the corpus (or reverting the query model) puts both sides back in one vector space.
- ✗ **B. Prompt filtering:** the problem is in retrieval, before the model sees anything. A prompt cannot make the right chunk appear when the search never returns it.
- ✗ **C. Bigger chunks:** chunk size affects precision and context, but it did not change here. The drop began when only the query model changed, and larger chunks would still be compared across two vector spaces.
- ✗ **D. More chunks:** retrieving more neighbours from a broken similarity ranking adds more unrelated text. It raises token use and noise without restoring relevance.

## Key idea
Embed queries and documents with the same model; after a model change, re-embed the corpus before switching queries.
Q004658:
## South or north of the Ontology
Palantir describes the Ontology as the semantic layer between data pipelines and applications. Work **south** of it runs in pipelines and publishes data into object properties. Work **north** of it runs at interaction time, in functions, agents and apps.
## Choosing the layer
The exam guide asks you to justify the layer with consumer breadth, freshness, reusability, scale and cost.
- South: many consumers need the same result, the input is large, a nightly refresh is fresh enough. Compute once, validate, store, reuse.
- North: the reasoning depends on the user's current context or question, so it cannot be computed ahead of time.
- Auditability: for batch enrichment, keep the prompt and the raw response next to the parsed output so wrong labels can be traced and reprocessed.
Example: a category used for filtering by five apps is computed once per ticket in the pipeline; "draft a reply to this customer given what I just wrote" belongs north.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Generate on view:** every view repeats the same LLM call, so cost grows with traffic, the label is missing for filters and dashboards that never open the ticket, and two views can return different labels.
- ✓ **B. Batch step in the pipeline (correct):** one reusable label per ticket, needed by many consumers, at large scale and nightly freshness, is exactly the case for south-of-Ontology processing. Structured output and validation keep the property usable for filtering, and stored prompts and responses support audits.
- ✗ **C. Classify inside the agent:** labels would exist only inside conversations. Other apps could not filter on them, and 2 million tickets cannot be processed through chat sessions.
- ✗ **D. One function per app:** each team gets different labels for the same ticket, the work is repeated for every app, and nothing is validated or stored for audit.

## Key idea
Reusable, large-scale enrichment that many consumers need runs south of the Ontology; context-dependent reasoning for one user runs north.
Q004659:
## Why one run is not enough
Model outputs are non-deterministic: the same input can produce a different answer on another run. On 50 cases, one case is 2 points, so a 3-point gap can be just one or two cases flipping by chance.
## Separating three explanations
The exam guide asks you to tell apart a real regression, expected variance and a change in the test distribution.
- Variance: run each version several times on the same suite and look at the spread of scores.
- Regression: the candidate fails the same cases consistently, ideally cases of one kind (for example, every multi-step calculation).
- Distribution change: confirm the suite, evaluators and target function were identical for both runs.
Example: if the current model scores 87-92% over five runs and the candidate 86-90%, the gap is inside the noise; if the candidate always fails the four unit-conversion cases, that is a real regression in one area.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Revert on any drop:** a single-run difference of one or two cases can be noise. Reverting without evidence may discard a better model.
- ✗ **B. New self-graded suite:** changing the test set at the same time as the model makes the two scores incomparable, and letting the candidate grade its own answers biases the result.
- ✓ **C. Repeated runs and case inspection (correct):** measuring run-to-run spread shows whether 3 points is signal, and looking at which cases change shows whether the failures are systematic. Holding the suite fixed rules out a distribution change.
- ✗ **D. Five-point rule:** no fixed threshold separates noise from regression; it depends on suite size and variance. A consistent failure on a small group of cases can be a real regression even at 3 points.

## Key idea
Before calling a regression, measure variance with repeated runs on a fixed suite and inspect which cases change.
Q004660:
## Where duplicates come from
Automate runs effects when a trigger fires, and it can retry when a step fails or times out. A timeout does not always mean the work failed: the Action may have finished after the caller stopped waiting. A retry then runs the whole chain again and creates a second record.
## Idempotent writes
An operation is idempotent when running it twice has the same effect as running it once.
- Give the write a natural key, here the invoice: one invoice, at most one payment request.
- Check for an existing request (or a stored operation status) before creating one; if it exists, return it instead of creating another.
- Keep retries: they recover from genuine temporary failures, which is why you make the write safe rather than removing them.
The exam guide asks for workflows that stay safe when an AI call, Action or external dependency fails or is retried.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disable retries:** genuine temporary failures would leave invoices unprocessed, and a manual weekly catch-up delays payments. The real defect, an unsafe write, stays in place.
- ✗ **B. Prompt instruction:** the extraction model does not create the payment request; the Action does. A prompt cannot enforce a data constraint at the write boundary.
- ✗ **C. Longer timeout:** timeouts and retries can still happen for other reasons, such as an overloaded dependency, and every retry would still create a duplicate.
- ✓ **D. Idempotent Action (correct):** keying the payment request to the invoice and checking before creating makes every retry harmless, so temporary failures are still recovered without duplicate payments.

## Key idea
When a workflow retries, make every write idempotent so a repeated run cannot duplicate its effect.
Q004661:
## Reading a trace for latency
A trace lists each step with its duration. Here two things dominate:
- Three independent retrieval calls run one after another, so their times add up. Independent steps can run in parallel.
- A 60,000-token prompt: model latency and cost grow with input tokens, and low-relevance chunks add noise that can lower answer quality.
## Targeted optimization
The exam guide asks you to profile the trace and recommend a targeted optimization rather than simply choosing a larger model. Typical levers are fewer or parallel calls, smaller and more relevant context, caching where safe, and asynchronous execution for genuinely long work. After any change, run the regression evaluation to confirm quality, safety and cost did not get worse.
Example: tightening retrieval to the top relevant chunks could cut the context to around 8,000 tokens, and parallel retrieval removes two sequential waits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nightly batch:** users ask new questions interactively; precomputed answers cannot respond to them. Asynchronous work suits long jobs, not a few-second assistant.
- ✓ **B. Parallel retrieval and smaller context (correct):** these are the two bottlenecks the trace shows. Both reduce latency directly, and trimming irrelevant chunks often improves grounding too; the evaluation run checks that quality holds.
- ✗ **C. Larger model:** larger models are usually slower and more expensive per token. It does nothing about the sequential retrievals or the oversized context.
- ✗ **D. More capacity:** the trace shows workflow structure and prompt size as the cost, not queuing at the provider. Capacity would not shorten sequential calls or a 60,000-token input.

## Key idea
Profile the trace first: parallelize independent steps and cut irrelevant context before reaching for a bigger model.
Q004662:
## What prompt injection is
Prompt injection hides instructions inside data the model reads, here an email. A model cannot reliably tell the user's instructions from text inside the content it was asked to process, so any tool it holds can be triggered by an attacker who controls that content.
## Enforce controls outside the prompt
The exam guide is explicit: do not rely on prompts to enforce policy; enforce least privilege at the data, retrieval, tool, Action and execution boundaries, and add human review for high-consequence actions.
- Least privilege: a summarizer needs to read, not write. Remove the write tool from this agent.
- Separate recommend from execute: the agent may suggest a change; an Action with validation (allowed ranges, required fields) performs it.
- Human review: credit limits are high-consequence, so a person approves.
With these in place, a successful injection can at most produce a misleading summary, not a financial change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Read-only agent and an approved Action (correct):** taking the write tool away removes what the attacker wants to trigger, and the separate Action enforces validation and approval at the boundary where the change happens.
- ✗ **B. Prompt rule:** instructions in the prompt can be overridden or confused by injected text; they reduce risk at best and cannot be the main control for a financial write.
- ✗ **C. Log and reverse later:** auditing detects damage after it happened. The unauthorized credit-limit change still takes effect and may be used before anyone reverses it.
- ✗ **D. Phrase blocklist:** attackers can reword the instruction in endless ways. Keyword filters miss variants and give a false sense of safety.

## Key idea
Treat content as untrusted: limit tools to what the task needs, and put validation and human approval on high-consequence Actions.
Q004671:
## Typed inputs and outputs in AIP Logic
AIP Logic functions declare their inputs and outputs with types: strings, numbers, booleans, enumerations, lists, object references and structs. The output type is part of the function's contract: whatever consumes the function receives that shape, not whatever the model happened to write.
## Why this matters for automations
An automation or a Workshop app cannot negotiate with prose. When the output is typed, a priority that is not one of the three allowed values fails inside the function, where it can be retried or surfaced, rather than breaking the consumer later.
- Enumerated output: the priority can only be low, medium or high.
- Numeric output: the confidence is a number, not "about 80%".
- The consumer reads fields, so a wording change in the model's reasoning cannot break it.
Example: output `{priority: high, confidence: 0.82}` works for every consumer; the sentence "I would rate this as High (82%)" works only until the model phrases it differently.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lower temperature:** less randomness makes the format more consistent but does not guarantee it; the consumer still parses prose and still breaks on any variation.
- ✗ **B. JSON in the prompt:** asking for JSON in prose still leaves the model free to add text or malformed JSON, and the consumer still carries the parsing and validation burden.
- ✗ **C. Regular expression:** pattern matching on free text is brittle; a sentence such as "not high priority, confidence low" produces the wrong priority and the wrong number.
- ✓ **D. Typed structured output (correct):** the contract moves from "parse whatever the model says" to "the function returns this structure", which removes the format drift that causes the failures.

## Key idea
Give an AIP Logic function a typed output; consumers should receive a structure, not text to parse.
Q004672:
## Single completion versus tool-using reasoning
AIP Logic offers two ways to use the model:
- A **single completion** sends one prompt with the injected inputs and takes the answer. It is fast, cheap and predictable.
- A **tool-using reasoning** block lets the model decide, over several steps, which tools to call (Ontology queries, functions, other Logic) before answering. It is for tasks where the needed information is not in the inputs.
## Matching the block to the task
The exam guide asks you to choose single completion or tool-using reasoning appropriately. Summarizing text that is already an input needs no lookup. Giving the model tools anyway adds latency per step, cost per call, and a new failure mode: calling tools it does not need and pulling unrelated data into the answer.
Example: "summarize this transcript" is a completion; "summarize this transcript and link each action item to the owner's open tasks" would justify tools.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More iterations:** this lets the model make even more tool calls, so runs get longer and the chance of unrelated data in the summary rises.
- ✓ **B. Single completion without tools (correct):** the transcript is already an input, so the model has everything it needs. Removing the tools removes the slow steps and the irrelevant lookups at the same time.
- ✗ **C. More tools:** the function would gain more ways to fetch data the task does not need; the problem is that tools are present at all, not that two are missing.
- ✗ **D. Larger model:** a stronger model may pick tools more sensibly but is slower and dearer, and it still cannot make an unnecessary lookup useful.

## Key idea
Use tool-using reasoning only when the answer needs data that is not in the inputs; otherwise a single completion is faster, cheaper and more predictable.
Q004673:
## Deterministic logic or AI
The exam guide's first decision area is whether a task is a fixed, reproducible rule or needs interpretation. "Amount greater than 10,000" is a rule. Letting a language model apply it means accepting a small error rate on something that never needed judgement.
## Blocks in AIP Logic
A Logic function is a sequence of blocks: completions, tool calls, conditionals, loops and edits. A **conditional** branches on a typed input or on an earlier block's output. Here the amount is a typed number, so the branch is evaluated exactly, and the model only does the part that needs language: writing the note in the chosen template.
This also makes the function easier to test: each branch can be checked with a claim on either side of the threshold.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Conditional block on the amount (correct):** the threshold becomes deterministic code inside the function, and the model is only asked to write text within the template that the branch selected.
- ✗ **B. Run twice:** this doubles cost and latency and still relies on the model to apply the rule; two guesses are not a guarantee.
- ✗ **C. Threshold tool:** fetching the rule from a tool makes it configurable, but the comparison is still performed by the model rather than by code.
- ✗ **D. Emphasize the rule in the prompt:** the rule stays a request to the model, so it can still be missed; prompt emphasis reduces errors but does not remove them.

## Key idea
Put fixed rules in conditional blocks; reserve the model for the parts that need language or interpretation.
Q004674:
## Applying Ontology edits safely
An Ontology edit from a Logic function changes real objects that people and automations rely on. The exam guide asks you to apply Ontology edits safely: an edit should depend on the object's current state, not only on the incoming evidence.
## Allowed transitions
Order statuses usually form a state machine: New → Shipped → Delivered, with Cancelled as a terminal state. "Cancelled → Shipped" is not a valid transition no matter what an email says. A conditional block can read the current status before the edit block runs:
- allowed transition: apply the edit;
- not allowed: skip the edit and flag the order so a person can check whether the cancellation or the shipment is wrong.
Example: an email for order 1182 (status Cancelled) is logged as "shipment reported for cancelled order", not written as Shipped.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Daily batch:** a cancellation can still happen after the daily run, and delaying every status update by a day harms the normal case without fixing the conflict.
- ✗ **B. Append to notes:** this avoids the overwrite but stops the function from doing its job for the normal case, so every shipment would need a manual status update.
- ✓ **C. Precondition on current status (correct):** the edit is only applied for valid transitions and conflicting evidence is routed to review, which is exactly the "edit safely" pattern.
- ✗ **D. Prompt instruction:** the model does not see the current status unless the function provides it, and a prompt rule can be misapplied; the guard belongs in logic that reads the object.

## Key idea
Before an Ontology edit, read the object's current state and only apply transitions that are allowed; send conflicts to review.
Q004675:
## When code is more suitable than AIP Logic
The exam guide asks you to understand when code is more suitable than AIP Logic. AIP Logic is for tasks that need language understanding or flexible interpretation. Three signals point to code here:
- **Determinism**: currency conversion with fixed rounding rules has exactly one correct answer per input.
- **Scale**: two million rows per night is a pipeline-scale batch, where per-row model calls would be slow and expensive.
- **Scheduling and control**: a nightly job with rate limits and programmatic control is what Code Repositories are for.
A language model is not a calculator: even at temperature zero it can produce wrong arithmetic, and it cannot be audited the way a rounding function can.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Code in a repository (correct):** deterministic arithmetic at batch scale on a schedule is the textbook case for a transform or function, giving exact results, testability and low cost.
- ✗ **B. Loop block:** looping two million completions through a Logic function is slow and expensive and still trusts the model with exact arithmetic.
- ✗ **C. Agent with calculator:** an agent adds reasoning, latency and cost to a task with no judgement in it, and the calculator tool does the only part that matters.
- ✗ **D. Logic with temperature zero:** zero temperature makes output more repeatable, not correct; model arithmetic and rounding errors remain, and two million completions a night are costly.

## Key idea
Deterministic, large-scale, scheduled computation belongs in code; AIP Logic is for tasks that need language or interpretation.
Q004676:
## Tuning parameters
AIP Logic exposes model parameters such as temperature and maximum output tokens. **Temperature** controls randomness: higher values let the model pick less likely tokens, which helps creative writing and hurts classification. A classifier should be as deterministic as possible, so a low temperature is the first setting to change.
## Constrain the output type
A typed enumerated output removes a second source of variation: the model cannot answer "mostly shipping, maybe billing" when the contract is one of six values. Together, low temperature and an enumeration make repeated runs far more consistent.
After tuning, rerun the evaluation suite several times; the remaining spread tells you how much variance is still inherent to the model, which matters when you judge future changes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More retrieved context:** a classifier of review text needs no retrieval; extra context adds noise and makes behaviour depend on which neighbours were returned.
- ✗ **B. Three runs, keep the last:** the last answer is no more reliable than the first, and three completions triple the cost without reducing randomness.
- ✓ **C. Low temperature plus enumerated output (correct):** the two settings target the two causes of run-to-run variation, randomness in generation and freedom in the output format.
- ✗ **D. More output tokens:** longer explanations do not make the final label more stable; they add cost and give the model more room to wander.

## Key idea
For classification, lower the temperature and constrain the output to the allowed values before changing anything else.
Q004677:
## Versions in AIP Logic
A Logic function is edited as a draft and released by **publishing** a version. Consumers (Workshop, Automate, other functions) use a published version, so editing and publishing are separate steps. The exam guide asks engineers to publish versions and preserve behaviour for existing consumers.
## A safe release
- Make the change in the draft and run the evaluation suite against it.
- Publish it as a new version; the earlier version keeps serving current consumers.
- Update the consumers one by one, checking each; if something breaks, that consumer goes back to the earlier version.
This is the same discipline as software releases: new behaviour ships behind a version boundary, and rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency edit.
Example: the new output field is added in version 4; the Workshop app moves first, the two automations the following week after their owners confirm the new field.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Point consumers at a draft:** drafts change while being edited; consumers would follow every keystroke, which is the opposite of preserving behaviour.
- ✗ **B. New function and delete the old:** this duplicates the function's identity, breaks every reference to the old name on deletion and loses the version history.
- ✗ **C. Edit in place:** every consumer would receive untested behaviour at once, and there is no version to fall back to if the reworded prompt changes results.
- ✓ **D. New version, evaluate, migrate consumers (correct):** the previous version keeps working while the change is tested, and each consumer is switched only when its owner is ready.

## Key idea
Publish changes as a new version, evaluate, then migrate consumers deliberately while the old version stays available.
Q004678:
## Loops over typed lists
AIP Logic blocks include **loops**, which run a set of blocks once for each element of a list input or of an earlier block's output. Each iteration gets its own completion with just that element injected into the prompt, and the results are collected.
## Why one giant prompt fails
Putting hundreds of items into one prompt hits token limits, raises cost, and makes quality drop as the model's attention is spread across the whole list. Per-item completions are bounded in size regardless of the order, and a single bad item does not spoil the notes for the others.
Example: an order with 380 lines becomes 380 short completions, each with the same template and one item injected, returning a list of 380 notes in the same order.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recursion on failure:** retrying halves after failures is unpredictable, wastes the failed attempts and is not a supported design for a Logic function.
- ✓ **B. Loop block per item (correct):** it fits the data shape (a list of independent items), keeps every prompt small and produces a typed list output the consumer can use.
- ✗ **C. Split orders upstream:** changing the data model to work around a function design corrupts the order's identity and still does not bound the prompt for a mid-sized order.
- ✗ **D. Maximum context:** larger context raises cost and latency and only postpones the limit; quality on very long prompts still degrades.

## Key idea
Process a list of independent items with a loop block, one bounded completion per item.
Q004679:
## Standard agents versus AIP Assist
AIP Agent Studio builds **standard agents**: purpose-built assistants with their own instructions, retrieval context and tools, which can be embedded in Workshop, exposed standalone or used in AIP Studio. **AIP Assist** is the platform-wide helper for questions about using Foundry itself; it is not a place to wire custom business tools into a specific app.
## Choosing the channel
The exam guide asks you to distinguish the two by deployment context and capabilities, and to use Workshop embedding, standalone access and AIP Studio appropriately.
- Embedded in Workshop: the agent can use the module's state (what is on screen) and its Actions, so dispatchers stay in one place.
- Standalone: good for general assistants that do not depend on an app's context.
Example: "why is shipment 4471 late and who can take it?" needs the board's objects and its reassignment Action, which the embedded agent can call.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Standalone page:** a separate tab loses the application state and forces dispatchers to describe what they are looking at; integration with the board's Actions is weaker.
- ✓ **B. Embedded standard agent (correct):** it lives where the dispatchers work, sees the board's shipments and can propose reassignments through the same Actions, with tools scoped to that domain.
- ✗ **C. Scheduled Logic function:** a daily list is not an assistant; it cannot answer questions in the moment or react to the current board.
- ✗ **D. AIP Assist:** it answers questions about the platform, not about a company's shipments, and it cannot be given the dispatch board's Actions.

## Key idea
For an assistant that works with an app's objects and Actions, build a standard agent and embed it in that Workshop module.
Q004680:
## Tools define what an agent can do
An agent's tools are its capabilities: every tool is a thing the model can decide to call. The exam guide asks why the agent needs these tools, and says to give a system only the tools, data and Actions the task requires.
## Why fewer, narrower tools are safer and better
- Safety: a policy question answerer with a delete-record tool can be manipulated into deleting a record; without that tool the worst outcome is a wrong answer.
- Quality: the model chooses among tools on every turn; fifteen overlapping tools make wrong choices more likely and slow each turn.
- Separation: reading policy and changing a record are different consequences; the change belongs in an Action with validation and a human in the loop.
Example: tools become "search leave policy", "look up my remaining balance"; "request a leave record change" opens an Action that HR approves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger model:** a better model still has fifteen tools and a delete capability it should never have had; it reduces one symptom without fixing the design.
- ✗ **B. Instruction only:** an instruction does not remove a capability; the model can still call a delete tool when confused or manipulated, and tool choice stays cluttered.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Narrow, read-only tool set with a reviewed Action for changes: the agent keeps what the task needs, loses the capabilities that make misuse dangerous, and chooses tools more reliably.
- ✗ **D. No tools at all:** some tools are useful and safe (reading a balance); the principle is least privilege, not zero capability.

## Key idea
Give an agent only the narrow, mostly read-only tools its task needs; put changes behind controlled Actions.
Q004681:
## Grounding and the refusal path
A retrieval-grounded agent should answer from the evidence it retrieved. The exam guide's self-check asks what the agent should do when the evidence is insufficient: it needs an explicit behaviour, such as saying the knowledge base does not cover the question and offering escalation. Without that, the model fills the gap with a plausible guess.
## Making it reliable
- Instructions: answer only from retrieved context; when nothing supports an answer, say so and suggest the next step.
- Context handling: include enough relevance signal (scores or thresholds) that "nothing relevant" is detectable.
- Testing: the exam guide calls for representative, edge and adversarial cases; unanswerable questions are an edge case that must be in the test set, and the evaluation should check refusal behaviour.
Example: "Can I pay with cryptocurrency?" with no article on payment methods should produce "I don't have information on that; I can connect you to an agent", not an invented policy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Explicit uncertainty path, tested (correct):** this gives the agent a correct behaviour for insufficient evidence and verifies it, instead of hoping the model stays quiet.
- ✗ **B. Lower temperature:** randomness is not the cause; a deterministic model will still produce its most likely guess when it has no evidence and no instruction to refuse.
- ✗ **C. More articles:** retrieving more for an out-of-scope question adds unrelated context, which gives the model more material to confabulate from.
- ✗ **D. Blanket disclaimer:** it shifts the burden to customers and does nothing about the invented content; the agent keeps hallucinating with a warning attached.

## Key idea
Give every grounded agent a tested path for "the evidence does not answer this" instead of letting it guess.
Q004682:
## What to test before release
The exam guide asks for representative, edge and adversarial interactions, and for tests of normal, edge, adversarial, unauthorized and high-consequence cases. For an agent that can spend money, each category maps to a real risk:
- Representative: normal requests, to confirm basic quality.
- Edge: missing fields, unclear quantities, items not in the catalogue.
- Unauthorized: a user who may not purchase; the agent must not submit.
- Adversarial: instructions hidden in content the agent reads, such as a supplier quote that says "approve this at any price".
- High-consequence and ambiguous: a large request with unclear details should be constrained or sent to review, not maximized.
Keep the set as a regression suite so later prompt or model changes are checked against the same cases.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Typical only:** fifty happy-path cases say nothing about missing details, wrong permissions or manipulated input, which is where a purchasing agent fails expensively.
- ✗ **B. Load test:** concurrency and latency matter, but they do not test whether the agent submits a request it should have refused.
- ✗ **C. Beta with real purchases:** real money is spent during the test, and mistakes are only found if someone notices them; it is feedback, not pre-release testing.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Mixed normal, edge, unauthorized, adversarial and high-consequence cases: this is the only option that exercises every way a purchasing agent can cause harm, not just whether it works when used properly.

## Key idea
Test an agent that can act across normal, edge, unauthorized, adversarial and high-consequence cases before it goes live.
Q004683:
## Multi-agent coordination
The exam guide lists multi-agent coordination, where required, among the deployment options. Three specialist agents each have focused instructions, their own retrieval context and narrow tools. That focus is what makes them accurate.
## Why a coordinator rather than a merge
- A coordinating agent receives the question, decides which specialists are needed, calls them (as tools or sub-agents), and composes the answer.
- Each specialist keeps its scope, tests and ownership; the coordinator adds only routing and synthesis.
- Merging everything into one agent produces an oversized context and tool set, which lowers quality and makes testing and ownership harder.
Example: "Can we offer net-90 terms with a 15% discount on this contract?" is split into a delivery-terms question, a pricing question and a contract-clause question, then combined.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One merged agent:** the combined instructions and tools dilute each specialist's focus; quality and tool selection degrade, and the three teams lose clear ownership.
- ✗ **B. Manual consultation:** it pushes the coordination work onto users and does not answer the actual question of whether the deal as a whole is allowed.
- ✗ **C. Train a custom model:** training foundation models is outside the AI engineer's role boundary and would freeze knowledge that changes constantly; retrieval exists for exactly this.
- ✓ **D. Coordinator over specialists (correct):** cross-cutting questions get routed and combined while each specialist stays small, accurate and separately maintained.

## Key idea
When questions span several specialist agents, add a coordinating agent rather than merging them into one.
Q004684:
## Conversation behaviour
Agents keep the turns of a conversation so that "it still fails after the restart" refers to the device and error mentioned earlier. That state belongs to the session: it should not leak into other users' sessions, and it should not be confused with the retrieval corpus.
## Separating memory kinds
- Session context: the current conversation, needed for follow-ups.
- Retrieval corpus: curated, governed knowledge that every user may see, maintained deliberately.
- Feedback: resolved conversations can inform improvements, but through a review process that strips personal details and checks quality, not by automatic appending.
The exam guide lists conversation behaviour and guardrails among the things to configure, and the security domain requires sensitive data to stay within its permissions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Auto-append to corpus:** unreviewed conversations with personal details would become retrievable by everyone; corpus changes need curation and permission checks.
- ✗ **B. No history:** every follow-up would need the user to repeat the device and error, which makes the agent nearly unusable for troubleshooting.
- ✓ **C. Per-session state without cross-user sharing (correct):** follow-up questions work, and nothing one user said becomes visible to another.
- ✗ **D. Shared memory of all conversations:** other users' device details, names and errors would surface in unrelated chats, which is a data-protection failure.

## Key idea
Keep conversation state inside the session; feed knowledge back into the corpus only through a reviewed process.
Q004685:
## Enforce access at the data boundary
The exam guide is explicit: do not rely on prompts to enforce policy; retrieval must return only authorized evidence, and the execution context must be verified. If a tool can query any customer's orders, the model can be asked, tricked or simply confused into doing so.
## How to scope it
- Run tools under the user's own permissions, so the Ontology returns only objects that user may see.
- Constrain the tool's query itself to the user's customer (for example, a filter the model cannot remove).
- Verify in tests that an unauthorized request returns nothing, regardless of phrasing.
Example: the same question after the fix yields "I can only show orders for your company" because the search finds no other rows at all.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Permission-scoped retrieval and tools (correct):** the data the agent can reach is limited at the source, so no phrasing of the question can produce another company's orders.
- ✗ **B. Output filter:** scanning for names misses amounts, product lines and paraphrases; the unauthorized data was already retrieved and processed.
- ✗ **C. Static nightly summaries:** this removes useful live data and still needs correct per-user scoping of which summary each user may see.
- ✗ **D. Prompt rule:** the capability remains; a reworded request or an injected instruction can still trigger the query. Prompts reduce risk; they do not enforce access.

## Key idea
Scope what an agent can retrieve to what the user is allowed to see; never leave authorization to the prompt or to output filtering.
Q004686:
## From pilot to production
A pilot gives evidence about ten users' questions. Company-wide use brings new question types, new documents and adversarial inputs. The exam guide treats a polished demo as insufficient evidence and asks for designs that are testable, observable and operated with monitoring.
## Controlled release
- Regression suite: the pilot's representative, edge and adversarial cases, run on every later change.
- Staged rollout: a department at a time, so a problem affects a bounded group.
- Observability: traces, feedback and cost reviewed as the audience grows.
- Rollback criteria: decided before release (for example, groundedness below a threshold, or any unauthorized data in answers).
Example: week one, legal and procurement; week three, all of operations, after the trace review shows no grounding regressions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rewrite on a new model:** discarding the tested agent at release time throws away the pilot's evidence and introduces untested behaviour at the moment of widest exposure.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Regression suite, staged rollout, monitoring and rollback criteria: these turn the pilot's evidence into a controlled expansion rather than a leap.
- ✗ **C. All at once:** the pilot covered a narrow population; a defect found at full scale affects everyone, with no plan for pulling back.
- ✗ **D. Remove tools for a month:** if the tools are needed, the release is no longer the agent that was tested; if they are not, they should not be there at all.

## Key idea
Expand an agent in stages, with the pilot's cases as a regression suite, monitoring, and rollback criteria set in advance.
Q004687:
## Chunking
An embedding represents the meaning of a whole text. A 40-page procedure embedded as one vector captures its general topic, not the torque value on page 23. Retrieval then finds the right document, and the model receives tens of pages where the detail is buried.
## Chunk design
The exam guide lists chunking, metadata, embedding and vector-property strategies. Practical rules:
- Chunk by logical units (sections, steps) so a chunk is self-contained; keep the heading so "Bolt M12 torque: 45 Nm" stays attached to its component.
- Attach metadata (procedure id, equipment, revision) to filter and to cite.
- Store chunk vectors (for example as a vector property on a chunk object) and retrieve chunks, then pass only those to the model.
Example: the torque question now retrieves the "Rear axle: fastener torques" chunk and the answer is in a few hundred tokens of context.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Prompt instruction:** the model cannot quote what it cannot find in a long context reliably; the fix belongs in retrieval, not in a request to look harder.
- ✗ **B. Larger embedding model:** a better model still has to compress 40 pages into one vector; the granularity problem is in the chunking, not the model.
- ✗ **C. More whole documents:** this multiplies the irrelevant text; the detail is still buried, now in several documents instead of one.
- ✓ **D. Section-level chunks with headings and metadata (correct):** retrieval becomes precise enough to return the passage that holds the detail, and the model's context is small and relevant.

## Key idea
Chunk long documents into self-contained sections with metadata so retrieval returns the passage that holds the answer.
Q004688:
## Precision, recall and context budget
Recall asks whether the right chunk is in the retrieved set; precision asks how much of the set is relevant. Retrieving 40 chunks raises recall but fills the context with near-duplicates from similar products. The exam guide warns that more context can add noise, conflict, staleness or unauthorized data, and asks you to balance precision, recall, freshness, token limits and latency.
## Better levers than "more"
- Metadata filters: restrict the candidate set to the product named in the question before ranking by similarity.
- Smaller top-k with a relevance threshold.
- Reranking the candidates so the most specific chunks come first.
Example: "maximum load of model X200" filtered to product = X200 returns five chunks, none about the X210, and the mixing disappears.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 80 chunks:** this makes the noise and the product mixing worse and raises latency and cost; the issue is precision, not recall.
- ✓ **B. Fewer chunks plus a product metadata filter (correct):** precision rises because other products' chunks are excluded before ranking, and recall for the right product stays high within a small, relevant set.
- ✗ **C. Bigger context window:** fitting more noise is not the goal; the model still has to disambiguate similar products from conflicting chunks.
- ✗ **D. Prompt-level filtering:** the conflicting chunks are still in the context; asking the model to ignore them is unreliable and wastes the token budget.

## Key idea
Improve retrieval with filters and ranking, not by retrieving more; more context often means more noise.
Q004689:
## Freshness in retrieval
A retrieval corpus is only as current as its index. If a document is replaced but the chunk objects and their vectors from the old version remain, both versions are retrievable and the old one may rank first because it matches older phrasing. The exam guide lists freshness among retrieval criteria and asks you to diagnose whether poor answers come from chunking, embeddings, ranking, thresholds, context selection or generation.
## What to check
- Does the chunk pipeline delete or supersede chunks of replaced documents, or only append?
- Do chunks carry a version or effective-date property that retrieval can filter on?
- Is there a transaction or build that shows the new chunks exist and are embedded?
Example: the lineage shows chunks for policy v3 and v4 both present; adding a "current version" filter and removing superseded chunks fixes the answers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model memory:** the assistant quotes the rule from retrieved context, not from training; changing models leaves the stale chunks in place.
- ✗ **B. Prompt preference rule:** the model cannot reliably tell which chunk is newer without version metadata, and the superseded text should not be in the corpus at all.
- ✓ **C. Stale chunks still indexed (correct):** a replaced document whose old chunks remain is the direct cause of answers citing the old rule; inspecting the chunk pipeline and version metadata confirms and fixes it.
- ✗ **D. More chunks:** both versions would appear and the model would have to guess; the fix is to stop retrieving superseded content.

## Key idea
When answers cite outdated content, check whether superseded chunks are still indexed; freshness is a retrieval problem before it is a prompt problem.
Q004690:
## Separating retrieval from generation
A RAG workflow has stages: chunking, embedding, ranking, thresholds, context selection and generation. The exam guide asks you to identify which stage to change and how to measure the improvement. Measuring retrieval separately is exactly what this team did: 95% of questions have the right chunk in the top five.
## Reading the two numbers together
High retrieval hit rate with low answer accuracy points downstream:
- Context assembly: is the correct chunk actually included in the prompt, in a readable order, or cut off by a token limit?
- Prompt: does it tell the model to answer from the context and cite it?
- Generation: is the model ignoring the evidence, or is the question type (calculations, comparisons) beyond what the prompt supports?
Example: the trace shows the correct chunk at position five was dropped when the top three were passed to the model; passing all five fixes most failures.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Context assembly and generation (correct):** retrieval is measured and healthy, so the failure sits between "chunk retrieved" and "answer produced", which the trace of the prompt and the model's output reveals.
- ✗ **B. Lower threshold:** admitting more chunks adds noise to a context that already contains the right one; it does not fix how that chunk is used.
- ✗ **C. Embedding model:** the embeddings already find the right chunk 95% of the time; changing them risks the part that works.
- ✗ **D. Smaller chunks:** a high hit rate does not indicate chunks are too large; re-chunking changes a working stage without evidence.

## Key idea
Measure retrieval and generation separately; when retrieval is good and answers are bad, fix context assembly and the prompt.
Q004691:
## Two kinds of evidence
Not everything should go through a vector search. The exam guide's context-injection strategy covers how evidence reaches the model, and the Ontology already holds exact facts as properties.
- Unstructured: manual text has no fixed schema; semantic search over chunks finds the relevant passage.
- Structured: model, location and last service date are properties of the Machine object; reading them directly is exact, cheap and permission-aware, with no similarity ranking involved.
## Assembling context
The workflow looks up the machine object, injects its properties, retrieves manual chunks for that machine's model (a metadata filter), and passes both. Provenance stays clear: facts come from the object, procedures from the manual.
Example: "When was pump P-17 last serviced and how do I replace its seal?" uses the property for the date and the seal-replacement chunk for the procedure.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Embed everything:** turning exact properties into sentences and searching them semantically makes precise facts fuzzy, and a similarity search may return another machine's date.
- ✗ **B. Properties only:** procedures live in the manuals; without them the assistant cannot explain how to do anything.
- ✓ **C. Semantic search for text, direct property reads for facts (correct):** each kind of evidence is fetched by the method that is exact and efficient for it, and the context carries clear provenance.
- ✗ **D. Infer facts from manuals:** manuals do not contain a specific machine's service date; the model would guess.

## Key idea
Retrieve unstructured text with semantic search and read structured facts straight from the object; combine both in the context.
Q004692:
## Trading precision, recall and latency
The exam guide asks you to balance precision, recall, freshness, token limits and latency. Two costs stand out here: reranking 200 candidates with a second model, and a 30-chunk prompt. Both scale linearly with their counts.
## A measured reduction
- Reranking fewer candidates (50) keeps most of the benefit, because the right chunk is usually well inside the top 50 by similarity.
- Passing fewer chunks (10) shortens the prompt and often improves answers by removing noise.
- The evaluation set tells you whether recall dropped; if it did, adjust the numbers rather than guess.
Example: rerank 50, pass 10 brings latency to about 2.5 seconds with no measurable loss on the evaluation set; the team keeps the reranker, which protects precision.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Answer cache:** legal questions rarely repeat exactly, so most requests miss the cache and the seven-second path remains for them; caching also risks stale answers.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Smaller rerank set and fewer passed chunks, verified by evaluation: both bottlenecks shrink and the reranker's precision benefit is kept; the measurement shows whether recall survived.
- ✗ **C. Search only recent chunks:** legal answers often depend on older documents; silently excluding them trades correctness for speed.
- ✗ **D. Drop the reranker:** this removes the stage that most improves precision in legal search and still passes a 30-chunk prompt; quality loss is likely and the prompt stays slow.

## Key idea
Reduce rerank candidates and passed chunks in measured steps rather than removing stages or restricting the corpus.
Q004693:
## Chunk size and similarity
A short chunk about one topic produces a vector very close to a short query on that topic. A long chunk averages many topics, so its vector sits further from any single query. Mixing 100-token and 800-token chunks therefore biases ranking towards the short ones, regardless of which document is actually best.
## Fixing it
The exam guide lists chunking strategy as the first thing to design and to suspect when retrieval misbehaves.
- Choose one chunking strategy (size, overlap, by section) and apply it to the whole corpus, or make sizes comparable.
- Re-embed after re-chunking, then run the retrieval evaluation set to confirm manual questions retrieve manual chunks again.
- Use metadata (document type) in filters if some question types should prefer one source.
Example: re-chunking manuals to around 150-200 tokens by step restores the expected ranking without touching the model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Two indexes:** splitting the corpus forces a routing decision per question and still leaves the size skew inside each index.
- ✗ **B. Date penalty:** recency is not what the vector search ranks on; a date penalty would be a workaround that also harms genuinely recent, relevant bulletins.
- ✗ **C. Long-document embedding model:** the bias comes from chunk length, not the model; re-embedding only one part of the corpus with a different model breaks comparability entirely.
- ✓ **D. Inconsistent chunk sizes (correct):** the symptom appeared exactly when a very differently chunked set was added, and short chunks win on similarity; a consistent strategy plus re-evaluation fixes it.

## Key idea
Keep chunking consistent across a corpus; mixed chunk sizes distort similarity ranking.
Q004694:
## Provenance in context injection
The exam guide asks that retrieved evidence expose its provenance to the workflow and that AI systems provide audit and lineage evidence. Provenance has to be carried, not reconstructed: if the chunks go into the prompt as anonymous text, nothing downstream can say which one mattered.
## Design
- Inject each chunk with a stable identifier (chunk object id, document, section, version).
- Make the output typed: answer text plus a list of supporting chunk ids.
- Validate that the cited ids are among the retrieved ones, so the model cannot invent a citation.
- Show the citations to the user and store them with the answer for audit.
Example: "Replace the seal every 2,000 hours [chunk 8812: Pump P-series manual, section 4.3, rev 7]".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Identified chunks and structured citations (correct):** the supporting evidence is named by the workflow at the point where it is known, validated against what was retrieved, and recorded for audit.
- ✗ **B. Model recall of names:** without identifiers in the context the model would guess document names; invented citations are worse than none.
- ✗ **C. List everything retrieved:** this does not say which chunk supported the answer and buries the real source among irrelevant ones.
- ✗ **D. Store the answer only:** a record of answers without their sources does not meet the requirement to show what supported each one.

## Key idea
Carry chunk identifiers through the context and return them as structured citations; provenance must be tracked, not remembered.
Q004695:
## Processing documents with LLMs and VLMs
The exam guide lists batch LLM processing, entity extraction, visual document processing and structured output among the data-processing capabilities. Scanned and photographed invoices have no reliable text layer, so a **vision-capable model** reads the page image directly.
## Making extraction trustworthy
- Structured output: define the three fields and their types so the model's answer is parsed into columns, not prose.
- Validation: dates must parse, totals must be numeric and plausible, suppliers can be matched against a known list; failures go to a review queue.
- Auditability: keep the prompt and the raw model response next to the parsed values (see the auditability task), so a wrong total can be traced.
Example: 300,000 pages run as a scheduled batch; 2% fail validation and are routed to a reviewer rather than silently written.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Visual document processing with structured output and validation: it reads images directly, produces typed columns, and catches bad extractions before they reach consumers.
- ✗ **B. File names only:** names rarely hold the total or the correct date; the real values are on the page image, which this approach never reads.
- ✗ **C. Regex on bytes:** scanned PDFs contain image data, not text; regular expressions have nothing to match, and even text invoices vary too much for fixed patterns.
- ✗ **D. Conversational confirmation:** 300,000 invoices cannot be confirmed one by one in chat; this is a batch workload for the pipeline.

## Key idea
For scanned documents, use vision-capable extraction with structured output and validation in a batch pipeline step.
Q004696:
## Auditability of AI outputs
The exam guide asks to preserve prompts and raw responses where auditability and debugging require them. An LLM label is the result of three things: the input, the prompt (and its version) and the model. If only the label survives, nobody can explain or reproduce it later.
## What to keep
- Prompt version or hash, model identifier, and parameters.
- The raw response before parsing, which shows what the model actually said.
- A timestamp and the pipeline build that produced the row.
Storage is cheap relative to a compliance finding, and the same data makes debugging possible when quality drifts.
Example: the auditor sees the raw response "Category: billing (customer disputes a double charge)" produced by prompt v12 on model X, which explains the label without re-running anything.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Post-hoc reason:** a second model explaining a label it did not produce is a rationalization, not evidence of the original decision.
- ✗ **B. Re-run on request:** models are non-deterministic and the prompt and model have changed in two months; a re-run shows today's behaviour, not what happened then.
- ✗ **C. Keep inputs only:** inputs without the prompt, model and response do not explain the label; re-classification by auditors produces a different result.
- ✓ **D. Stored prompt, model and raw response per label (correct):** this reconstructs how the label came to be, exactly as it happened, without relying on reproduction.

## Key idea
Preserve the prompt version, model and raw response next to every AI-generated value that may need to be explained later.
Q004697:
## North and south again
The exam guide's layering rule: south of the Ontology for reusable batch enrichment, north for interactive, context-dependent reasoning. The deciding factors are consumer breadth, freshness, reusability, scale and cost.
## Why this is north
- The question is different each time and unknown in advance, so there is no reusable result to compute ahead.
- The context must be current: the orders and tickets as they are at that moment.
- One analyst asks, and the answer is used once.
A function (AIP Logic or code) or an agent is invoked when the analyst asks, fetches the customer's objects under the analyst's permissions and reasons over them.
Example: "Why has this customer's ticket volume doubled since the last order?" cannot be precomputed; a batch summary would not address it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hourly general summary:** a generic summary is not an answer to a specific question and goes stale within the hour.
- ✓ **B. Interaction-time function north of the Ontology (correct):** the reasoning depends on the live question and current objects, which is the case the guide reserves for the north layer.
- ✗ **C. Precomputed likely questions:** the analyst's question is not in a fixed set; stored answers would be stale and usually off-topic.
- ✗ **D. Annotate at ingestion:** annotating each record with an answer to an unknown future question is impossible and would bloat every sync.

## Key idea
Context-dependent, one-off reasoning over current objects runs north of the Ontology at interaction time.
Q004698:
## When to codify a workflow
The exam guide names the triggers for moving AI processing into Code Repositories: scheduled batch execution, programmatic control, rate limiting, or libraries beyond what no-code tools offer. This case has all four.
## What the repository gives
- Scheduling as part of the pipeline, with builds and lineage.
- Code-level control over batching, concurrency and backoff, so the provider's rate limit is respected.
- Explicit retry and failure handling, with failed items recorded rather than lost.
- Declared dependencies, so the custom cleaning library is versioned with the transform.
Example: the transform processes reports in batches of 20, sleeps on rate-limit responses, writes summaries and a status column, and runs at 01:00 nightly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Agent on request:** an agent is an interactive tool; it is the wrong shape for an unattended nightly batch with rate-limit control.
- ✗ **B. Manual notebook:** a reminder is not scheduling; failures depend on someone watching, and nothing is versioned or reproducible.
- ✓ **C. Code Repositories transform (correct):** it provides scheduling, rate limiting, retries and custom libraries in one governed place, which is exactly the list of needs.
- ✗ **D. Single Logic loop:** a Logic function is not designed for scheduled large batches with custom libraries and provider-level rate control; one huge run is fragile.

## Key idea
Scheduled, rate-limited, retried or library-dependent AI processing belongs in a Code Repositories transform.
Q004699:
## Structured output needs constraints and validation
Structured output tells the model the shape of the answer. For a categorical field, the shape should include the allowed values: an **enumeration**. The exam guide pairs structured outputs with deterministic post-processing and quality checks.
## Defence in depth
- Enumeration: the model is asked for one of 40 values, not free text.
- Validation: anything that still does not match is rejected by code, not written; the row goes to a review queue or gets a null plus a status.
- Monitoring: the invalid rate is a quality metric; a jump signals a prompt, model or data change.
Example: "Sportswear" fails validation; the row is flagged, reviewed, and the reviewer's choice becomes a new evaluation case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Enumeration plus validation and review (correct):** the constraint prevents most invalid labels and the validation guarantees that none reach the dataset unchecked.
- ✗ **B. Fuzzy mapping:** "Sportswear" might map to "Apparel" or to "Sports equipment"; silently guessing hides errors in the data.
- ✗ **C. Accept new categories:** downstream filters and dashboards depend on the 40 categories; unplanned values break them and the taxonomy drifts without governance.
- ✗ **D. Prompt sentence only:** it lowers the rate but gives no guarantee, and without validation the remaining invalid labels still get written.

## Key idea
Constrain categorical AI output with an enumeration and validate in code; route failures to review rather than guessing.
Q004700:
## Caching in AI pipelines
The exam guide lists caching among the controls for AI data processing. An LLM call is deterministic enough in purpose, if not in wording, that regenerating a summary for unchanged input is pure waste.
## Incremental generation
- Key the cache on a hash of the input fields that the prompt uses (plus prompt version and model). Same key, same summary, no call.
- Process only new or changed records each night; 1% of 2 million is 20,000 calls instead of 2 million.
- Keep a periodic full regeneration or a prompt-version bump to refresh everything when the prompt or model changes.
This is also a data-engineering pattern: an incremental transform over the changed rows.
Example: a prompt change increments the version in the cache key, so every record regenerates once, then nightly runs return to 1%.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Weekly run:** this trades freshness for cost and still regenerates unchanged records every week.
- ✗ **B. Shorter summaries:** output tokens are a fraction of the cost per call, and the two million unnecessary calls remain.
- ✗ **C. Cheaper model:** the waste remains, since 99% of calls are still unnecessary; quality drops for no structural gain.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Cache keyed on input content and prompt version with incremental runs: cost drops to roughly 1% of today's with no loss of freshness or quality.

## Key idea
Cache AI outputs by input content and prompt version, and regenerate only what changed.
Q004701:
## Two workloads, two layers
The exam guide's rule is to justify each AI task's layer by consumer breadth, freshness, reusability, scale and cost.
- **Sentiment per transcript**: every transcript, needed by a dashboard for aggregation, the same value for every viewer, nightly freshness is fine. That is reusable batch enrichment: south, stored as a property.
- **"What is this customer unhappy about today?"**: a specific question, about current transcripts, for one user. That is interactive, context-dependent reasoning: north, computed when asked, and it can read the stored sentiment too.
Example: the dashboard aggregates `sentiment` over 80,000 transcripts in a query; the manager's question runs a function over the 6 transcripts from today for that customer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reversed:** this puts the aggregate workload on the interactive path and the one-off question in the batch, which is backwards on every criterion.
- ✓ **B. Batch sentiment south, on-demand question north (correct):** each workload lands where its breadth, freshness and scale point, and the north function can reuse the south result.
- ✗ **C. Both south:** the manager's question cannot be precomputed because it is not known in advance; stored answers would be stale and generic.
- ✗ **D. Both north:** computing sentiment for 80,000 transcripts every time the dashboard opens is slow and costly, and yields inconsistent values between views.

## Key idea
Aggregate, reusable scores go south as properties; specific, current questions are answered north on demand.
Q004702:
## Deterministic post-processing
The exam guide pairs AI processing with deterministic post-processing and quality checks. Extraction is the AI step; deciding that three spellings are one entity is a resolution step that should be rule-based and reproducible.
## Entity resolution in the pipeline
- Normalize: case, punctuation, legal suffixes ("Corp", "Corporation").
- Resolve against a reference list of known organizations, assigning the canonical id.
- Unresolved names go to a review queue; confirmed matches extend the reference list.
- The object's primary key is the canonical id, so a fourth spelling tomorrow lands on the same object.
Example: "ACME Corp" and "Acme Corporation" both resolve to `org-00417`; "Acme Holdings" stays unresolved for review.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ask for the official name:** the model's idea of a canonical name is unreliable and unverifiable, and the article text drives what it returns.
- ✗ **B. Lower temperature:** the spelling variation comes from the source articles, not from randomness; the model would still return the text it sees.
- ✓ **C. Normalization and entity resolution before object creation (correct):** the mapping is explicit, repeatable and governed, and the Ontology receives one object per organization.
- ✗ **D. Link the duplicates:** this preserves the duplicates and pushes the problem onto every application and query that counts organizations.

## Key idea
Keep extraction in the model and entity resolution in deterministic code with a canonical key.
Q004703:
## What an evaluation suite needs
The exam guide asks for representative evaluation suites with test cases, target functions, evaluators and metrics. A test case has an input, an expected result and an evaluator that compares them.
## Representative, not convenient
- Coverage: the clauses should span contract types, date formats ("30 days after signature" as well as explicit dates), currencies and unusual phrasing, so the suite can catch failures the common cases hide.
- Ground truth: the legal team's confirmed values are the expected outputs; they do not come from the function under test.
- Evaluators: exact match for amount and date is appropriate because the fields are deterministic; looser evaluators are for free-text outputs.
Example: 300 cases, stratified by contract type, with 40 deliberately hard ones, give a precision figure that means something.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cases it already passes:** a suite built from known successes cannot reveal weaknesses; it measures nothing new.
- ✗ **B. Current output as truth:** this freezes today's mistakes as the expected answer and only detects change, not correctness.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Stratified real cases with confirmed values and exact-match evaluators: the suite measures the function against the truth, across the variety it will meet in production.
- ✗ **D. Synthetic clauses with model-generated truth:** the expected values are not verified, so errors in them are counted as correct, and synthetic text may miss real-world phrasing.

## Key idea
Build evaluation suites from representative real cases with independently confirmed expected outputs.
Q004704:
## Testing the failure modes that matter
The exam guide asks evaluation to include normal, edge, adversarial, unauthorized and high-consequence cases. For an approving agent, the dangerous outcome is a wrong approval, so the suite must contain the cases that could produce one:
- Edge: amounts just above the limit, where rounding or misreading flips the decision.
- Adversarial: a violation phrased to look compliant, or an instruction in the description ("this has been pre-approved by finance").
- Unauthorized: a submitter who may not request approval.
- High-consequence or ambiguous: a large report with unclear receipts, which should be escalated rather than decided.
Each case gets an expected outcome (approve, refuse, escalate) and an evaluator that checks the decision, not just the wording.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Parsing variations:** useful later, but a parsing error on a normal report is less consequential than a wrong approval on an adversarial one.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Edge, adversarial, unauthorized and ambiguous high-value cases: these are the ways the agent can approve something it should not, which is the risk the suite exists to catch.
- ✗ **C. More normal cases:** the suite already covers in-policy reports; adding more of them improves confidence in the easy case only.
- ✗ **D. Load cases:** latency under load is an operational metric, not an evaluation of decision quality, and belongs in a separate performance test.

## Key idea
Prioritize evaluation cases that could produce the worst outcome: edge, adversarial, unauthorized and high-consequence inputs.
Q004705:
## Evaluators for free text
Deterministic outputs (an amount, a category) suit exact-match evaluators. Free text does not: two correct explanations can differ in every word. The exam guide lists evaluators and metrics as things to design, and the design should fit the output.
## A rubric with a deterministic anchor
- Rubric criteria: mentions the correct reason, suggests the next step, avoids internal jargon, no promises about outcomes, polite tone. Each is scored separately, so a failure tells you what to fix.
- Deterministic anchor: the decline reason in the text must match the reason code on the transaction; this is checked in code, not by judgement.
- Model-based grading can score rubric items, but it needs explicit criteria and should be spot-checked against human ratings.
Example: a case fails "correct reason" when the text says "insufficient funds" but the record says "card expired", regardless of how well written it is.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Rubric per criterion plus a deterministic factual check (correct):** this measures the qualities that matter, points to the failing criterion, and anchors correctness to the record.
- ✗ **B. Exact match:** a different but correct wording would fail; the metric would measure phrasing, not quality.
- ✗ **C. Single "looks good" judgement:** an unstructured verdict is inconsistent and cannot say what is wrong; it also misses factual mismatches that a model may not notice.
- ✗ **D. Human review of everything:** humans calibrate the automated evaluator and review samples, but reviewing every output does not scale to continuous regression testing.

## Key idea
Evaluate free text with criterion-level rubrics and anchor factual claims with deterministic checks.
Q004706:
## Three causes of a score change
The exam guide asks you to distinguish a genuine regression, expected variance and a change in the test distribution. Changing the prompt and the suite in the same week mixes two of them.
## Separating the effects
- Hold the suite fixed: on the original 200 cases, old and new prompts both score 94%, so the prompt did not regress on that distribution.
- Look at the new 40 cases alone: both prompts should be run on them. If both score low, the cases are a harder or different distribution (or need label review); if only the new prompt scores low, there is a regression specific to that kind of input.
- Report the two numbers separately rather than one blended score.
Example: both prompts score 50% on the 40 new multilingual cases; the suite now covers something the function never handled, which is a gap to work on, not a regression.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Normal variance:** a nine-point drop concentrated entirely in the new cases is not run-to-run noise; it is a signal about those cases.
- ✗ **B. Revert and remove cases:** the evidence does not show a regression on the original data, and removing hard cases hides a real gap.
- ✗ **C. Assume mislabelling:** new cases can be mislabelled, but a lower score on a different sample is also what a genuine coverage gap looks like; check, do not assume.
- ✓ **D. Distribution change to be separated from the prompt change (correct):** the unchanged 94% on the original cases shows the drop comes from the new cases, so each effect must be measured on its own before deciding anything.

## Key idea
Never change the suite and the function in the same comparison; measure old and new cases separately to tell distribution shift from regression.
Q004707:
## Closing the loop
The exam guide asks for feedback loops that capture user corrections or downstream outcomes and turn them into new evaluation cases or improvement priorities. Feedback is raw signal; it becomes useful when it is reviewed, turned into a reproducible test, and ranked.
## The process
- Review: some thumbs-down are wrong (user disagreement with a correct answer); confirm each failure.
- Convert: each confirmed failure becomes an evaluation case with the input, the retrieved context if relevant, and the corrected expected output.
- Prioritize: group failures by type (retrieval miss, refusal where an answer existed, wrong tool); fix the most frequent or most harmful first.
- Verify: every fix is checked against the growing suite, so old failures cannot return unnoticed.
Example: 60% of confirmed failures are retrieval misses on one document family; that becomes the first improvement, and its 25 new cases guard the fix.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Auto-append to prompt:** unreviewed feedback (including wrong feedback) would change behaviour immediately, bloat the prompt and bypass any testing.
- ✗ **B. Shrink scope on KPI:** a thumbs-down rate without diagnosis does not say what to fix; cutting scope removes value instead of correcting failures.
- ✗ **C. Weekly retraining:** training foundation models is outside the AI engineer's role; the practical levers are prompts, retrieval, tools and evaluation.
- ✓ **D. Review, convert to evaluation cases, prioritize by frequency (correct):** feedback drives measurable improvement and the suite grows to protect against regressions.

## Key idea
Turn user feedback into reviewed evaluation cases and prioritized fixes; it is signal to test against, not a control to react to blindly.
Q004708:
## Comparing models on non-deterministic outputs
Both the function and the grading model are non-deterministic, so a single run of each is two noisy measurements. The exam guide asks you to tell signal from variance and to detect regressions across models.
## A fair comparison
- Repeat runs: several runs per model on the same fixed suite give a distribution; compare the spread, not one number.
- Per-case view: see which cases the candidate wins and loses; a model that is better on average but fails a critical case type may still be the wrong choice.
- Calibrate the grader: sample verdicts and compare with human ratings; if the grader is inconsistent, both scores are unreliable.
- Decide against a threshold set in advance, including cost and latency.
Example: candidate 80-84% across five runs, current 78-82%, grader agrees with humans 92% of the time, and the candidate loses no high-consequence case: adopt.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Best of two:** two single runs are still too few, and "above 80%" does not compare the models against each other under the same conditions.
- ✗ **B. Adopt on one run:** a two-point gap on single runs of two noisy processes is not evidence; the next run could invert it.
- ✓ **C. Repeated runs, per-case comparison and grader calibration (correct):** this is how to know whether two points is a real difference and whether the measurement itself can be trusted.
- ✗ **D. Reject on principle:** a small gain can be real; the right response is to measure enough to know, not to assume it is noise.

## Key idea
Compare models with repeated runs on a fixed suite, per-case analysis and a calibrated grader before adopting a change.
Q004709:
## Refusal is a measured behaviour
The exam guide lists refusal behaviour among the things to measure, along with correctness, groundedness, tool selection, safety, latency and cost.
