- ✗ **D. Single score:** a 6 out of 10 does not say whether the answer was too long, uncited or promised a date; nothing is attributable.

## Key idea
Build evaluators per requirement, using deterministic checks wherever the requirement allows.
Q005216:
## Unauthorized-case design
The exam guide lists unauthorized cases among those to test and asks for object-state assertions. Authorization can fail at several points: identity, role, impersonation.
## Cases
- Requester without rights: expected refusal.
- Text claiming authority ("approved by the CFO"): expected refusal; the text is data.
- Requests on behalf of others: expected routing to the right approver.
- Assertion: no approval object or state change created.
Example: a contractor's request is refused and logged; no approval exists afterwards.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Identity, role and impersonation cases with no-change assertions: the ways authorization can be bypassed are tested directly.
- ✗ **B. Large amounts:** a high-consequence case, not an authorization case.
- ✗ **C. Only valid:** assumes permissions are perfect; the workflow's own checks must be tested.
- ✗ **D. Capital letters:** a formatting robustness case; it says nothing about whether the workflow checks who is asking.

## Key idea
Test unauthorized requests across identity, role and impersonation, asserting that nothing is approved.
Q005217:
## Suites are data too
The exam guide asks you to separate regression from test-distribution change. Edited expected answers change the suite; the function may be unchanged.
## Steps
- Diff the suite version before and after the edits.
- Verify the new expected answers against the source of truth (documentation, domain experts).
- Version control the suite; review changes like code.
Example: the new member "corrected" 20 expected answers using outdated policy; reverting them restores the score, and the release is fine.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Release broke it:** possible, but the coincidence with the edits must be checked first.
- ✗ **B. Grader broken:** a grader failure would not be confined to edited cases.
- ✗ **C. Provider change:** a model change would shift results across many case types, not land exactly on the cases a new colleague edited.
- ✓ **D. Review the suite edits first (correct):** a score drop confined to edited cases points at the suite, not the release.

## Key idea
Version evaluation suites and review changes to expected answers like code.
Q005218:
## Structured feedback capture
The exam guide asks for feedback loops that convert corrections into evaluation cases and priorities. A bare rejection cannot be converted into anything.
## Capture
- Reason category: wrong fact, missing info, tone, unsafe, other.
- Corrected output (optional).
- Input reference and trace id.
- Aggregation by category → fixes and cases.
Example: 60% of rejections are "missing info"; retrieval k is raised and 25 cases added; rejections halve.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reject only:** a count of rejections with no reasons cannot be turned into a fix or a test case.
- ✓ **B. Structured reasons with corrections and references (correct):** rejections become analyzable and actionable.
- ✗ **C. Thumbs-up only:** silence is ambiguous (not reviewed, or rejected?) and there is no information about what was wrong.
- ✗ **D. Mood:** the reviewer's state of mind does not explain what was wrong with the output; it is noise.

## Key idea
Capture structured reasons and corrections with each human rejection.
Q005219:
## Evaluating open-ended text
The exam guide asks for evaluators that fit the output. Summaries with legitimate structural variation need content-based rubrics, not similarity to a single reference.
## Rubric
- Must-include facts (per case); must-exclude (hallucinations).
- Length bounds; clarity criterion.
- Model-graded with calibration; disagreements reviewed.
Example: two summaries with different structure both pass because they contain the five required facts and nothing false.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No evaluation:** whether the five required facts are present and nothing false was added is objective and measurable.
- ✗ **B. Exact match:** two correct summaries almost never match word for word; the metric would fail nearly every valid output.
- ✗ **C. Similarity to a reference:** penalizes valid summaries that differ in form.
- ✓ **D. Content-based rubric with calibration (correct):** measures what matters (facts, no fabrication) and tolerates legitimate variation.

## Key idea
Grade summaries on required content and absence of fabrication, not on similarity to one reference.
Q005220:
## High-consequence cases
The exam guide asks for high-consequence cases with escalation as the expected outcome. Bulk deletion is irreversible and broad.
## Case
- Input: "delete all records with status X".
- Expected: the agent reports the count, asks for confirmation (or escalates above a threshold), and deletes nothing yet.
- Assertion: record count unchanged after the turn.
Example: "This would delete 4,120 records. Do you want me to proceed?" with no deletion until confirmed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rename one:** a reversible change to one record; the consequence is minimal and no escalation is expected.
- ✗ **B. List only:** a read-only preview; useful as a normal case, but it cannot test how the agent behaves when asked to destroy data.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** A broad deletion request expecting scope disclosure and confirmation with no change: the archetypal high-consequence case.
- ✗ **D. Policy question:** an informational answer; nothing is at stake beyond a possibly wrong explanation.

## Key idea
Test destructive bulk actions with cases that expect confirmation and no change.
Q005221:
## Shift evaluation left
The exam guide asks for regression detection across changes. Finding regressions at release time is the most expensive moment.
## Practice
- Fast tier on every commit or draft publish.
- Full suite nightly and before release.
- Failures fixed while the change is fresh.
Example: a prompt change that regresses multilingual cases is caught the same afternoon it is made.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Continuous fast evaluation with nightly full runs (correct):** regressions surface when introduced, not on release day.
- ✗ **B. Skip:** the regression that was caught would instead have reached every user; avoiding a slip by shipping a defect is no improvement.
- ✗ **C. Ten cases:** a suite that small cannot cover the behaviours that regress; speed is bought with blindness.
- ✗ **D. After release:** users experience the regression first and the suite merely confirms what they already reported.

## Key idea
Evaluate continuously during development, not only at release.
Q005222:
## Suite curation
The exam guide asks for representative suites and sustainable regression testing. Size is not coverage; near-duplicates add cost without information.
## Approach
- Deduplicate by similarity; keep one per cluster.
- Stratify: categories × difficulty; ensure coverage.
- Archive: full historical set for periodic deep runs.
- Admission rule: new cases must add a new failure type or category.
Example: 3,000 cases become a 400-case core that runs in minutes and a 3,000-case archive run monthly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Start over:** years of real failure cases are discarded, and the regressions they guarded against can return unnoticed.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Deduplicated, stratified core with an archive and admission rules: coverage preserved, cost controlled.
- ✗ **C. Stop adding:** new failure types discovered in production would never be covered; the suite freezes while the system evolves.
- ✗ **D. Add forever:** near-duplicates multiply runtime without adding information until nobody runs the suite at all.

## Key idea
Curate evaluation suites for coverage, not size.
Q005223:
## Event-driven screening with a complete record
The exam guide asks for triggers matched to latency and for auditable workflows. A one-hour requirement means an event trigger; "record even when nothing is found" means the Action always writes.
## Configuration
- Trigger: Contract created.
- Effects: screening function → Action creating ScreeningResult (outcome, flags, version, time), unconditionally.
- Monitoring: contracts older than an hour without a result raise an alert.
Example: 120 contracts created today each have a ScreeningResult, 117 clear and 3 flagged, all within minutes.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Manual:** screening depends on the officer's availability, so the hour requirement is unmet, and cleared contracts get no record.
- ✗ **B. Weekly, flagged only:** misses the hour requirement and leaves no record for cleared contracts.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Object-creation trigger with an unconditional result write and a freshness alert: the time and completeness requirements are both met and monitored.
- ✗ **D. Nightly email:** misses the hour requirement and creates no stored records at all.

## Key idea
Use event triggers for time-bound per-object processing and always write an auditable result object.
Q005224:
## Concurrency between automations
The exam guide asks for workflows that stay safe under concurrent and in-flight changes. A race is resolved with a consistency check at the write, not with timing tricks.
## Design
- Capture the object's version (or relevant properties) during validation.
- The Action's precondition compares the current version with the captured one; mismatch → reject and re-validate.
- Alternatively serialize the two automations on the same object.
Example: the write is rejected once in a hundred runs because the status changed meanwhile; the workflow re-validates and writes correctly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Random delay:** reduces the frequency of the race; does not prevent it.
- ✗ **B. Disable the other automation:** it maintains the property for its own business reason; removing it trades one problem for another.
- ✗ **C. Night only:** the other automation may run at night too, and latency suffers.
- ✓ **D. Optimistic version checks in the Action with re-validation (correct):** stale writes cannot happen, and the workflow self-corrects.

## Key idea
Prevent races between automations with version checks at the write and re-validation on conflict.
Q005225:
## Pausing safely
The exam guide asks for safe modification of live workflows with attention to in-flight work and duplicates. A pause must be resumable without gaps or repeats.
## Design
- Pause: disable the trigger; objects keep arriving.
- Backlog: identified by state (for example, objects without a result record).
- Resume: process the backlog with idempotent writes; then re-enable the live trigger.
- Verify: no object without a result.
Example: 340 objects created during a 3-hour migration are processed in one backlog run; counts reconcile.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Delete and recreate:** loses configuration and history; the backlog is still unprocessed.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Resumable pause with state-based backlog, idempotent processing and verification: nothing is lost or duplicated.
- ✗ **C. Ask users:** some users will not see the email and integrations keep creating objects; a request is not a control.
- ✗ **D. Skip:** a compliance or business process that must cover every object cannot have a gap; those objects would never be processed.

## Key idea
Pause automations with a plan to process the backlog idempotently on resume.
Q005226:
## Property-scoped triggers
The exam guide asks for triggers that avoid unnecessary executions and loops. The condition names the property explicitly.
## Configuration
- Trigger: `financial_rating` changed on a Supplier.
- Scope: that supplier only.
- Guard: the assessment writes to different properties, or skips when the change came from itself.
Example: a rating downgrade on one supplier re-runs one assessment; an address edit on another runs nothing.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Trigger on the specific property with per-object scope and a loop guard: exactly the requirement, nothing more.
- ✗ **B. Manual:** rating changes are noticed late or not at all; the re-assessment depends on an analyst's attention.
- ✗ **C. Daily for all:** a rating downgrade waits up to a day, and thousands of unchanged suppliers are re-assessed needlessly.
- ✗ **D. Any change, all suppliers:** massive unnecessary work and a loop risk.

## Key idea
Scope automation triggers to the property that matters and guard against self-triggering.
Q005227:
## Fail loudly on contract breaks
The exam guide asks for versioned, evaluated changes and workflows that remain safe when a step misbehaves. A renamed variable is a contract change; silent defaults hide it.
## Safeguards
- Function: missing required input → error, not default.
- Automation: validate non-empty, well-formed results; route failures.
- Release: evaluation suite on the change; version bump; consumers informed.
Example: the renamed variable would have failed the suite and the automation's validation on the first run, instead of three days of empty outputs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Timeout:** the function returned quickly with an empty default; time was never the issue, and a longer wait changes nothing.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Loud failures, output validation and evaluated, communicated changes: the silent breakage becomes impossible.
- ✗ **C. Bigger model:** the variable was never injected; no model can produce the right output from a prompt that lacks the input.
- ✗ **D. Defaults are fine:** a default for a required input converts a bug into bad data.

## Key idea
Required inputs fail when missing; validate outputs; evaluate and announce contract changes.
Q005228:
## Request objects and asynchronous completion
The exam guide recommends asynchronous execution for long work with status visibility, and integration through Actions and automations.
## Design
- Action: create the request (inputs captured, status pending).
- Automation: generate, write, update status; failures set status failed with reason.
- Notification on completion; the form can be closed meanwhile.
Example: the user submits and goes to lunch; the report is on the request object when they return, with a notification.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Request object plus automation with status and notification (correct):** long work completes reliably without holding the user.
- ✗ **B. Browser:** the model, the data and the write to the request object all live server-side; a client-side model cannot do this.
- ✗ **C. User runs it later:** the user still has to wait two minutes somewhere; the system should do the work and tell them when it is done.
- ✗ **D. Synchronous:** a two-minute frozen form, lost if the user navigates away.

## Key idea
Model long AI requests as objects processed by automations with status and notification.
Q005229:
## Rate-aware orchestration
The exam guide lists execution modes and rate limiting among orchestration concerns. Per-object parallel execution ignores provider limits.
## Design
- Batch mode or a paced code step: calls per second bounded below the limit.
- Backoff on throttling; failed items recorded and retried in-window.
- Monitoring: throughput and failure rate.
Example: 50,000 calls paced at 90% of the limit complete in 2.5 hours with zero throttling failures.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More parallelism:** the provider's limit is fixed; tripling concurrency triples the throttling and fails even more runs.
- ✗ **B. Provider roulette:** daily switching gives inconsistent outputs and still ignores each provider's limit; it is not a design.
- ✗ **C. Next-day retries:** a third of objects wait a day, then throttle again.
- ✓ **D. Paced batch execution with retries (correct):** the limit is respected and the morning run completes.

## Key idea
Pace high-volume AI automations against provider limits with batched, rate-limited execution.
Q005230:
## Cross-team orchestration discipline
The exam guide asks for versioning, evaluation and clear ownership in orchestration. A multi-team chain needs explicit contracts and shared tests.
## Practice
- Typed contracts at each boundary; contract test cases.
- Version pinning; upgrades are deliberate.
- End-to-end regression run of the chain pre-release.
- Ownership and alert routing per step; runbooks.
Example: team B's change fails the contract test with team C's cases before release, and the fix is made before anything ships.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Freeze forever:** the functions serve changing business needs; a permanent freeze blocks every improvement to avoid coordination.
- ✗ **B. One team:** organizational fantasy; the contract discipline is what matters.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Boundary contracts, version pinning, end-to-end regression and clear ownership: changes in one team cannot silently break the chain.
- ✗ **D. Informal hope:** a chat message before a change is easily missed; it is not a practice that catches a broken contract.

## Key idea
Operate multi-team AI chains with contract tests, version pinning and end-to-end regression.
